title: Lenz's law and conservation of energy
topicTitle: Lenz's law and conservation of energy
notes: Lenz's law says the induced current takes the direction that opposes the change in flux which caused it. It is the reason for the minus sign in Faraday's law.
If the south pole of a magnet approaches a coil, the flux of that pole is increasing. The near face of the coil becomes a south pole so that it repels the approaching south pole.
If that south pole is pulled away, the flux decreases and the near face becomes a north pole, attracting the magnet and opposing the removal.
The opposition is to the change. A stationary magnet produces no change and no induced current, so there is no force from an induced current.

Pushing the magnet in against the repulsion takes mechanical work. That work is the energy which appears as the induced current's heating in the coil. If the induced current had attracted the magnet, the motion would accelerate and energy would appear from nowhere.
Eddy currents in a copper plate near a moving magnet oppose the motion and dissipate energy as heat. That is Lenz's law used as a brake.

summary: Lenz's law chooses the induced current so that it opposes the change in flux. An approaching south pole is met by a south face. The agent must do work against that opposition, and that work is the energy of the induced current. A stationary magnet induces nothing.

exercises.question: The south pole of a magnet is pushed toward a coil. Name the pole on the near face and say where the energy of the induced current comes from.
steps: South-pole flux through the coil is increasing.
The near face becomes a south pole and repels the magnet.
The hand pushing the magnet does extra work against that repulsion.
That work is the energy dissipated by the induced current.
exercises.answer: A south face. The energy comes from the work done pushing the magnet.
